Claudia Sheinbaum reversed Mexico's ban on fracking this week, dropping her predecessor's energy-sovereignty doctrine to cut the country's dependence on imported natural gas.

She announced that Mexico will consider "non-traditional" fracking techniques to boost natural gas production by 38%. She acknowledged that Pemex lacks the technology and may need to bring in private partners through mixed contracts. The shift breaks with Andrés Manuel López Obrador's purist approach to energy sovereignty, driven by Mexico's reliance on American pipeline imports for 77% of its natural gas.

Even as energy policy shifts, the government is putting growth ahead of price stability. The central bank cut interest rates to 6.75% despite inflation reaching 4.59%, but the decision split the board 3-2. Some members warned about oil price volatility from Middle East conflict while the majority pushed for further cuts. The split reflects disagreement about how to handle those risks.

Ms Sheinbaum also opened the first Economic Development Pole in Tlaxcala, backed by $540m in investment and over 5,000 jobs. The site covers 53 hectares, expanding to 96, and 80% of its space is already committed. It is the first project under Plan México, the government's plan to spread manufacturing investment beyond the north and the Bajío region.

The Senate ratified Roberto Velasco as foreign minister with 81 votes. At 38, Mr Velasco has already served as undersecretary for North America, where he helped negotiate the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) — useful experience as the trade pact comes up for review. Ms Sheinbaum also announced her first European trip, travelling to Barcelona for a progressive leaders' summit organised by Pedro Sánchez. The visit marks Mexico's first presidential trip to Spain in eight years.

Residents of San José Chiapa, Puebla, disrupted Ms Sheinbaum's housing events to protest a recycling plant, chanting "No to the recycler" and "Down with the dump." When officials tried to block them, tensions rose. Local opposition can disrupt even government-backed projects.

Morena faces candidate-selection rows and a membership crisis after electoral authorities struck out 160,000 member registrations. Montserrat Caballero, a former mayor of Tijuana, resigned, accusing the party of "lies and betrayals" and saying it had lost its essence. The strains suggest the party will be harder to manage as success breeds internal competition.

Omar García Harfuch, the security secretary, has become something of a folk hero. The Wall Street Journal reports he is Mexico's Batman: street vendors sell "Harfuchas" sweet bread, towels and blankets bearing his image. The trade follows his operations against organised crime, with vendors reporting strong sales especially among women aged 40-50. His popularity reinforces his position in the 2030 succession race.

Viktor Orbán lost power in Hungary this week after Peter Magyar's opposition party won a two-thirds parliamentary majority. The defeat removes Ukraine's main obstacle to EU integration — Mr Orbán had blocked both its accession negotiations and a €90 billion loan package.

Volodymyr Zelensky immediately congratulated Mr Magyar and said Ukraine was ready to "develop cooperation" with Hungary. Andrii Sybiha, the foreign minister, echoed him, promising "mutually beneficial cooperation" and pledging to "find solutions to old problems." The new Hungarian government has not yet taken office or announced policy, but the victory opens the way for faster progress on EU financing and accession.

The diplomatic opening comes as Ukraine reports progress in peace talks. Kyrylo Budanov, head of the presidential office, said negotiations were moving toward a settlement: "I don't think it will be long." He said American envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner might visit Kyiv next week, and noted that "they all understand the war needs to end."

On the battlefield, Ukraine kept advancing. General Oleksandr Syrskyi, the commander-in-chief, said Ukrainian forces had retaken 480 square kilometres and 12 settlements since late January. Ukrainian drones killed a record number of Russian soldiers in March, up 29% from February, while interceptor drones shot down more than 33,000 Russian drones.

But the economy is under strain. The National Bank of Ukraine sold nearly $4.8 billion in March — the highest intervention since December 2024 — bringing total sales since January to roughly $12 billion. Officials warned that reserves could run out within months at current rates; they have fallen from $57 billion to $51.9 billion.

The government is also struggling to pass legislation required by international lenders. Parliament approved only one of four IMF-required tax bills, failing to muster enough votes for the rest. The EU had already withheld about €1.5 billion from Ukraine's latest aid payment over unmet reform conditions. Yuliia Svyrydenko, the prime minister, met members of the Servant of the People parliamentary faction to win support for the remaining bills.
